Psychology: educational

Learning, guidance, educational difficulties and family–school relations.

What it does

Educational psychology studies how people learn and how best to teach, and applies that knowledge in schools, universities and families. It is concerned with the learning of all students: those with difficulties, those who are highly able and those who simply need to learn how to study.

Where it works

  • Educational guidance teams and school counselling departments.
  • Early intervention services for children aged 0 to 6.
  • Designing materials, evaluating programmes and training teachers.
  • Private practice and family associations.

What works according to research

  • Retrieval practice: trying to recall what has been studied, for example with questions or flashcards, consolidates memory far better than rereading.
  • Spaced practice: spreading study over several days is more effective than cramming the night before.
  • Feedback that is specific and timely, focused on the task rather than the person.
  • Explicit reading instruction, including the link between letters and sounds, and early detection of dyslexia.
  • Classroom climate and trusting relationships with teachers, which affect motivation and behaviour.

An example

In 2013 John Dunlosky and his team reviewed ten study techniques widely used by students. Highlighting and rereading, the most popular, turned out to be of little use. The two most effective were self-testing and spacing study out. It is a good example of how research can correct intuition.

Common myths

The idea that each student learns best when taught according to their "learning style" (visual, auditory or kinaesthetic) is widespread among teachers, but well-designed studies do not confirm it. Nor is there evidence that people are "right-brained" or "left-brained".

References

  1. Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J. y Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.
  2. Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D. y Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105–119.
  3. Hattie, J. y Timperley, H. (2007). The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1), 81–112.
